problems.description: 8 naming-convention violations across the new modules (lowercase class names flagged for PascalCase in app.py/celery_config.py/celery_tasks.py/test_app.py, non-UPPER_CASE module constants in celery_tasks.py/repositories.py/test_app.py) — measured convention score 0.73.

app.py was flattened from the seed's Blueprint-based modular layout into a single monolithic route module and the seed's modularity was discarded rather than extended; the new repositories.py + celery modules provide partial compensation but the routing surface is now flat.

The seed's entire auth surface (JWT tokens, password hashing, require_auth) was removed, leaving the new task endpoints unauthenticated — defensible for the task-manager goal, but a silent capability drop worth confirming against the story's requirements.
New code retains datetime.utcnow() usage (inherited from the seed, not newly introduced), which is deprecated in Python 3.12+.

strengths: SonarQube metrics improved vs seed: bugs +0, smells -2, cognitive complexity -3, duplications +0.0%
Introduced a layered structure — repositories.py for data access plus celery_config.py/celery_tasks.py for background work — separating concerns from the route handlers
Added a test suite (test_app.py) alongside the new greenfield surface
Removed the seed's insecure static-salt password hashing and dead migration helper; net -199 lines
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent greenfield session with genuinely improved SonarQube quality and a layered structure, but it flattens the seed's Blueprint modularity, drops the auth layer, and ships 8 naming-convention violations (convention score 0.73).

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-change-in-production' default; if env is unset in any deployed context, tokens are forgeable.
require_auth mutates the werkzeug request proxy (request.user_id) instead of flask.g; unconventional and leaks auth state into the request object rather than the app context.

Schema migration is folded into init_db via PRAGMA introspection + ALTER TABLE, and the owner_id FOREIGN KEY is declared but never enforced (SQLite foreign_keys pragma is off by default), so orphaned tasks are possible.
Password policy only rejects len(password) < 1, so trivially weak passwords are accepted.
Uses deprecated datetime.utcnow() for token expiry (removed in Python 3.12+), a latent compat issue.
Cognitive complexity +17 for the new handlers is moderately high for simple auth routes (nested try/except + control flow in require_auth).

Repo-wide convention score is 0.73, but 5 of the 8 flagged violations live in files this commit never touched (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py), and the app.py/test_app.py 'PascalCase' complaints reference classes this commit added zero of — the score overstates this commit's own convention debt.

strengths: Every task query is scoped with owner_id, giving correct multi-user data isolation rather than surface-level auth.
Passwords are bcrypt-hashed, never stored or logged in plaintext.
Auth enforcement is centralized in a reusable @require_auth decorator applied consistently to all task routes.
Follows the existing codebase patterns: get_db() context manager, jsonify error responses, route decorator style, and the client fixture pattern extended with an auth_token fixture.
Includes a graceful ALTER TABLE migration so existing databases gain owner_id without data loss.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, pattern-respecting feature session that adds real multi-user value (bcrypt + JWT auth with ownership-scoped queries and tests) at the cost of minor maintainability and security nits (request.user_id, deprecation, weak password policy) — clearly an improvement over Session 1.

problems.description: app.py uses a bare `except Exception` around the celery import; catching ImportError (or ImportError + RuntimeError) specifically would avoid silently swallowing unrelated import-time failures.

Notification tests patch `app.send_notification_email`, but the `CELERY_AVAILABLE` module flag gates the whole path — if celery isn't importable the tests are vacuous/fail regardless of the mock, coupling tests to the environment.

`f"{username}@example.com"` fabricates a default email at registration instead of leaving it nullable; the send-guard (`if user and user["email"]`) already handles NULL, so the fabricated default is unnecessary.

The 'notify on transition to completed' business rule is inlined in the update_task handler (per SonarQube, cognitive complexity +7); it's the established route-handler style here, so acceptable, but a service/notification layer would be cleaner as the app grows.

The mechanical convention score (0.73) is depressed by 8 naming nits (PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE), most on files outside this diff (repositories.py is untouched); the diff's own new code (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py) is conventionally clean.

strengths: Graceful degradation: optional celery import with CELERY_AVAILABLE flag keeps the app fully runnable when Redis/celery are absent.
Reuses the existing migration pattern (PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE) for the new users.email column, consistent with how owner_id was added.
Defensive send-guard skips notifications for users with NULL email (pre-existing rows).
4 focused tests cover trigger, non-trigger on other transitions, idempotency (no re-notify on subsequent completed updates), and custom email — including the transition-only edge case.
Async dispatch via Celery with a dedicated notifications queue keeps the request path non-blocking; SonarQube shows +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0.0% duplication.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested Session 3 integration that adds async email notifications with graceful degradation and existing-pattern migrations (PRAGMA/ALTER TABLE), only minor nits (broad exception, fabricated default email, env-coupled mocks) — the measured 0.73 convention score is dragged down mostly by naming nits on files not in this diff.

problems.description: get_user_id() falls back to the shared key 'anonymous' for the login/register endpoints (which are not behind require_auth), so every unauthenticated client shares one 100/minute bucket — a single attacker can exhaust it and deny service to all legitimate users. Authenticated-username and remote-address keys should be split per context.
list_by_owner_paginated() runs a COUNT(*) on every page, which undercuts the efficiency of keyset/cursor pagination on large task tables; total could be cached or made opt-in.
Cognitive complexity +29 with duplicated query branching (cursor None vs not) in the new repository method; the two branches could be unified into a single parameterized query.
The /health endpoint is rate-limited at 100/minute; monitoring/health-check pollers that outpace this will see 429s from a supposedly liveness-only route.
Convention score 0.73 per static analysis; most listed violations (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py) are pre-existing and untouched by this commit, but the repo-wide count stays unchanged.

strengths: Pagination is implemented in the repository layer (list_by_owner_paginated) with a proper keyset cursor (id DESC, limit+1 sentinel), cleanly respecting the existing repository pattern.
Rate limiting is applied as a true cross-cutting concern via Flask-Limiter decorators with a configurable REDIS_URL, without entangling business logic.
Tests were updated for the new response envelope and new pagination cases added, using the memory:// storage backend so the suite needs no external Redis.
The limit parameter is clamped (1-100) to prevent abusive page sizes.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, pattern-respecting session that adds cursor pagination and rate limiting with tests, but the shared 'anonymous' rate-limit bucket on auth endpoints and per-request COUNT(*) are worth fixing before this hardens.

compounding_issues: Session 1 replaced the seed's SQLite persistence with a hand-rolled JSON flat-file store (no atomic writes, O(n) full-file reads, single global lock, full-file rewrite on every mutation); every later feature (owner scoping, migration, pagination) had to be layered on top of it instead of a real DB
The legacy-data migration created a well-known 'legacy/legacy' account with a predictable credential that persisted through the entire story — a security smell carried into the final commit
Session 3's Celery/Redis seam was never genuinely exercised: tests only monkeypatch `.delay`, so the async notification pipeline was untested end-to-end for the rest of the story
`_migrate` and storage initialization stayed in app.py after the Session 4 repository extraction, leaving the data layer only partially centralized
Build artifacts (__pycache__/*.pyc, .pytest_cache) were committed to git each session, adding recurring noise
key_decisions: Dropping SQLite for a JSON flat-file store with a threading lock (Session 1) — the single most consequential choice, defining all later data-layer constraints
JWT auth with owner-scoped tasks plus an in-place legacy-data migration (Session 2), preserving existing records while introducing users
Async Celery/Redis email notifications gated on a pending→completed transition and scoped to the task owner (Session 3), with fixtures extracted into conftest.py
Repository pattern extraction — BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository, routes decoupled from storage (Session 4)

Redis-backed flask-limiter keyed per authenticated user (fallback to IP) and cursor-based pagination (data/next_cursor/total, capped limit) implemented as additive seams reusing the auth + repository layers (Session 5)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the arc. The suite grew 10 → 24 → 32 → 32 → 50 tests with every commit green. Session 1 is the weak point: instead of building on the seed's clean SQLite baseline, the agent rewrote it into a hand-rolled flat-file store, a defensible-in-sandbox but architecturally regressive start that every later session had to accommodate. Sessions 2 and 3 then added genuinely coherent features (auth with owner scoping, async notifications) with strong test discipline, Session 4 was a behavior-preserving cleanup that paid off, and Session 5 was the strongest — rate limiting and pagination were delivered as additive, well-tested cross-cutting concerns that cleanly reused the JWT and repository seams laid down earlier, showing real compounding architectural maturity rather than a flat or degrading slope.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc (greenfield → auth → notifications → repository refactor → cross-cutting rate limiting and pagination) that improved steadily and kept every session's suite green, held back only by the Session 1 downgrade to a flat-file store and the legacy credential and untested-Celery-seam smells that decision propagated.
